name: Ugare
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: Ugare is a tonal language, and we've found it impossible to really understand any aspect of its grammar without first getting a handle on the tone system. Tone is used not only to distinguish lexical morphemes, but also to make grammatical distinctions such as tense in the verb phrase and association (ownership, etc.) between two nouns. [...] Ugare has two tones, high and low. These sometimes end up on the same syllable, producing a rising or falling tone. A two-way contrast is quite easily observed in Ugare, as in the following pair of words: [Low tone ìgò 'pig' / High tone ígò 'pigs']
new_statements.citation: Cassetta, Pete & Lydia Cassetta. 1994. A Phonology of Ugare. Revised September 10, 1994. Unpublished manuscript (SIL Cameroon), 17 pp.
new_statements.locator: §5 Tone and §5.1 Tones, p. 9 (scan page 11 of 19); tone processes §5.2 p. 10; noun tone §5.3 pp. 10-11; verb tone §5.4 p. 12
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given anywhere in the only phonological description of the language. Ugare is described as a two-tone language (H, L; rising/falling contours when both land on one syllable; long vowels carry one tone or a contour), with automatic downstep after L within and across word boundaries and morphophonemic upstep. Noun stems (1-2 syllables) show four patterns H, L, HL, LH; verbs fall into a high-tone and a low-tone class with tense/aspect tone melodies. The words stress, accent and prominence do not occur in the manuscript.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant to stress. Tone residue noted by the authors: floating-tone morphemes underlying noun morphophonemics and tense/aspect forms remain to be identified; some noun stems appear toneless (L in isolation, H after a H prefix).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is described at the word level (noun stems with/without prefixes, verb forms) and across word boundaries (downstep). Nothing on phrase-level stress or intonation. Source is a 1994 SIL working paper explicitly labelled preliminary ('our knowledge is far from complete').
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes 'Ugare' (autonym; Ethnologue/Glottolog 'Mesaka', also Messaga, Iyon), ISO iyo, Glottolog mesa1245, spoken around Akwaya (Southwest Region, Cameroon) with speakers also in Benue State, Nigeria. No dialect is specified; the Cassettas' data come from their SIL Cameroon work up to 1994. Blench writes the name 'Ugarə'.

sources.note: Bibliographic only: one descriptive reference (Cassetta & Cassetta 1994 verb system, grammar_sketch, 45 pp.); alternative names Mesaka, Banagere, Iyon, Messaga, Messaga-Ekol, Messaka.

Nothing on stress; 'Mesaka is also a tonal language with two tones: high and low', citing Blench 2011; vowel length contrastive in sequences of similar vowels (both statements trace to Cassetta 1994).

sources.note: Nothing on stress or prosody beyond tone-marked data (H/L, contour tones on noun-class suffixes). States (p. 205) that Ugare's 'descriptive coverage is poor with grammatical sketches by Cassetta & Cassetta 1994a, b, c forming the only available sources so far', and gives the rogerblench.info URLs for those three manuscripts; new Ugare data collected 2020-2022 from speakers in Ikyogen (Benue State, Nigeria) and Buea (Cameroon).
